name: pimpl
intent: Keep a class's implementation details out of its public definition by holding them behind an opaque pointer, so that changing the implementation neither forces users to recompile nor breaks the ABI of already-compiled clients.
problem: Implementation details leak into the header: private data members fix the class's size and layout and private helper types drag their own includes along, so any internal change forces every user of the header to be recompiled - and in a distributed library it breaks clients that were compiled against the previous version.
context: Code with textual headers and a layout-sensitive ABI: published libraries and frameworks, widely included headers in large builds, classes whose internals churn (protocols, formats, feature growth) or whose implementation pulls in heavy, platform-specific or third-party dependencies. The same decision appears outside C++ as the opaque type of a C library, the non-exported implementation class of a managed module, or the hidden body of a value type in a language with a stable module interface.
benefits: Compilation firewall: private data members disappear from the header, so editing the implementation recompiles only the library unit - include cascades and their rebuild cost vanish for the class's users.

ABI stability: the handle's size and layout are fixed by a single pointer, so new data members can be added without breaking binaries that already link against the old version (the reason Qt and KDE libraries use d-pointers).

Dependency hygiene: the public header no longer includes the implementation's headers, so heavy, platform-specific or third-party types stop leaking into every translation unit that touches the class.
Ironclad information hiding: what clients cannot see they cannot depend on, so the implementation can be reorganised, replaced per platform, or rewritten without an interface change.

Value-like handles stay cheap to move: with a uniquely owned body the handle can be movable with a single pointer move, and copy semantics become an explicit design decision (deep clone or deliberate sharing) instead of an accident of the member list.
Templates and non-template cores can be separated: a thin template forwards to a non-parameterised implementation, which keeps the firewall even where the class itself is generic.
tradeoffs: One extra heap allocation per object and one pointer indirection per member access; cache locality worsens, and in-place variants that remove the allocation give up the ABI guarantee to do it.

Boilerplate and lifetime discipline: every public member needs a forwarding definition, and the destructor plus copy/move operations must be written where the body is complete - the rule of five becomes mandatory rather than automatic.

The default copy semantics disappear: a handle with a unique body is movable but not copyable, so callers of a formerly plain class get a source break unless copy or clone semantics are supplied deliberately.
Debugging and profiling get harder: values are one hop away from the object, debuggers show a pointer instead of the state, and inlining across the firewall is no longer possible.

Exception and move safety must be re-derived: body construction can throw (the handle's constructor is no longer trivially noexcept), and a moved-from handle holds no body, so every operation must define what a valueless object does.

The idiom is viral at the boundary: any template, inline function or exported signature that needs the body re-introduces the dependency, so the firewall only holds if the whole public surface avoids the hidden type.

participants.responsibility: Publishes the interface, holds the opaque pointer as its only state and forwards every operation to the body; because its layout is the pointer, implementation changes cannot alter its size.

Carries the data members, helper types and private functions that used to sit in the header; it is defined only in the implementation unit, so it can be changed, replaced or made platform-specific without touching the interface.
The single member that fixes the handle's layout and breaks the compile-time dependency; it is typed as a pointer (or a pointer wrapper) to the forward-declared body and never as the body itself.

Decides how the body is created, destroyed, copied and moved (unique ownership, raw pointer with out-of-line delete, shared or copy-on-write body) and therefore whether the handle is movable, copyable or neither.

Needed only when a body operation must call back into the handle's public or virtual interface; it adds a second link between the halves that must be maintained across moves, so passing the handle as a parameter is usually preferred.
The out-of-line constructor (or factory) defined where the body is complete; it constructs the body, establishes invariants and is the only place that knows how the implementation is created.

use_cases: A shared library or framework whose headers are shipped to third parties and whose ABI must survive patch and minor releases (the Qt/KDE d-pointer scenario).
A class included almost everywhere in a large C++ build, where moving its private members out of the header removes an include cascade and cuts incremental build time.
A class whose implementation depends on a heavy or platform-specific SDK, vendor header or third-party library that should not appear in the public include graph.
A class whose internal data members are expected to churn - feature growth, protocol or format support, tuning parameters - while the public interface and its binary contract stay fixed.
Wrapping a C library behind a stable C++ or managed facade, where the vendor's struct and its header must stay out of the consumer's code.
Exposing a type across a plugin or FFI boundary, where the binary side may never see the implementation's layout and can only hold an opaque handle.
Qt's public classes use d-pointers and QSharedDataPointer to hide private data while preserving binary compatibility across releases; use this when a framework's shipped C++ ABI must evolve.
KDE Frameworks' binary-compatibility policy recommends d-pointers for public library classes, so apply pimpl when private data and dependencies must change without changing exported object layout.
avoid_when: Application-internal classes in a build that is always rebuilt as a whole: plain private members are simpler and faster, and the firewall protects nothing that is shipped.

Small, frequently created or hot objects (nodes, iterators, container elements): the extra allocation and indirection cost more than the coupling saved - keep members inline and profile before considering an in-place variant.
When C++20 modules (or another compiler-enforced module interface) already hide non-exported entities: the include cascade is gone, so keep pimpl only if the ABI guarantee is still needed.
Types that must stay cheaply copyable value types or be usable at compile time in constexpr contexts: a hidden pointer body gives neither without extra machinery.
Cases where a pure abstract interface plus factory is the better fit (several implementations chosen at runtime): that removes the compile-time dependency without the manual pointer bookkeeping.
anti_patterns: Reflexive pimpl: every class gets a pointer and a forwarding method per operation, producing allocation-heavy, unreadable code with no ABI or build-time requirement behind it.

Inline destructor over an incomplete body, so the smart pointer's destructor is instantiated in client code - the classic 'invalid application of sizeof to incomplete type' error, or a broken ABI when it happens to compile.
Sharing one body between handles without saying so (a shared body used as silent copy-on-write): copies alias, mutation surprises callers, and thread-safety reasoning collapses.

Leaking the body through the API - returning it by value, exposing it as a public nested type, or using it in a signature or template argument - which restores exactly the dependency the idiom removed.

Hiding the polymorphic interface (virtual or protected members) inside the body, so derived classes can no longer override; those members belong to the deriver's interface, not to private implementation.
Dereferencing a moved-from handle: with a unique body the moved-from object is empty, and any member function that assumes a live body crashes or corrupts state.
design_principles: Information hiding: separate what clients are allowed to depend on from what they must not - hide the decisions most likely to change.
Separation of interface and implementation: the published definition is a contract, the body is a replaceable detail.
Stable dependencies: the public header depends on forward declarations and minimal includes rather than on the implementation's own dependencies.
Single responsibility: the handle owns the contract and the lifetime, the body owns representation and mechanics.
Open/closed: the implementation can be extended, replaced or made platform-specific without editing or recompiling its users.
best_practices: Declare the destructor (and copy/move operations) in the header and define them in the implementation file where the body is complete; with a unique body this is mandatory for the destructor, not merely tidy.
Decide and document copy semantics explicitly: delete them, deep-copy with a clone function, or share the body deliberately as copy-on-write.
Keep the body's definition in the implementation unit only - a private nested type or a file-local type - and never mention it in a public signature, return type or template argument.
Make the handle movable with noexcept operations (a pointer move) and define the moved-from state (null body or a valid empty body) in the class contract.
Pass the handle into body functions instead of storing a back pointer; only a shared d-pointer hierarchy that genuinely needs the reverse link should pay for a q-pointer.
Keep profiling-sensitive accessors out of the body so they can still be inlined, and let the firewall cover the parts that actually churn.

If the per-object allocation is the problem, profile first and then consider in-place storage (Fast Pimpl) with static_assert checks on size and alignment, accepting that the buffer size becomes part of the ABI.
sources: Coplien, Advanced C++ Programming Styles and Idioms (1992) - the handle/body idiom, cited as the pattern's ancestor by Sutter (GotW #100).
Sutter, Exceptional C++ (2000) and More Exceptional C++ (2002) - the pimpl and compilation-firewall items; see also GotW #28 'The Fast Pimpl Idiom' and GotW #100 'Compilation Firewalls'.
